title: “There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous” (Psalm 14:5) and “…where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee” (Psalm 53:5)
summary: Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 are nearly the same psalm. Where Psalm 14:5–6 says that God is in the generation of the righteous and that the wicked shamed the poor man’s counsel, Psalm 53:5 says that God scattered the bones of the one who encamped against his people and put them to shame.
text: KJV Psalm 14:5: “There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous.” KJV Psalm 14:6: “Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 14:5–6: שָׁ֤ם ׀ פָּ֣חֲדוּ פָ֑חַד כִּֽי־אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים בְּדֹ֣ור צַדִּֽיק׃ / עֲצַת־עָנִ֥י תָבִ֑ישׁוּ כִּ֖י יְהוָ֣ה מַחְסֵֽהוּ׃. KJV Psalm 53:5: “There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 53:6: שָׁ֤ם ׀ פָּֽחֲדוּ־פַחַד֮ לֹא־הָ֪יָה֫ פָ֥חַד כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֗ים פִּ֭זַּר עַצְמֹ֣ות חֹנָ֑ךְ הֱ֝בִשֹׁ֗תָה כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֥ים מְאָסָֽם׃. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA014.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA053.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/14/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/53/.
reasoning: After the same opening, the two psalms diverge. Psalm 14 gives two short lines: the wicked feared, because God is with the righteous generation; the wicked shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge. Psalm 53 gives one longer line in which there was fear where no fear was, God scattered the bones of the one encamped against the people, and the one addressed has put them to shame because God has despised them. The Lord (Hebrew יְהוָה) is the refuge in 14:6, while the divine name used throughout Psalm 53 is God (אֱלֹהִים). The two psalms differ in who shamed whom: the wicked shamed the poor man’s counsel in 14:6, and the encamped enemy were put to shame in 53:5.
scope: This sets two psalms beside each other as the KJV gives them. It does not say either is in error. The psalms may be two forms of one song, and the books do not say which came first. The difference in the divine name, Lord against God, is a known feature of this group of psalms and is not claimed as a contradiction. Only the KJV and the Hebrew wording of these verses were compared; the Greek of Psalms 14 and 53 was not read in full, and Psalm 14:3 has its own published record. Psalm 53’s verse numbers in the Hebrew text run one higher than the KJV’s because the heading is counted as verse 1. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “The foundations also of the hills moved” (Psalm 18) — “the foundations of heaven moved” (2 Samuel 22)
summary: The same line of David’s song reads in the KJV of Psalm 18:7 “the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken”, and in 2 Samuel 22:8 “the foundations of heaven moved and shook”. Hills and heaven are different things.
text:
Preserved draft text:
KJV Psalm 18:7: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth.” KJV 2 Samuel 22:8: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:8 (the Hebrew count includes the title as verse 1): וַתִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַתִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָאָ֗רֶץ וּמֹוסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ כִּי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃ Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:8: [וַתְגָּעַשׁ כ] (וַיִּתְגָּעַ֤שׁ  ק) וַתִּרְעַשׁ֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ מֹוסְדֹ֥ות הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַיִּֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ כִּֽי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 17:8: Καὶ ἐσαλεύθη, καὶ ἔντρόμος ἐγενήθη ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὰ θεμέλια τῶν ὀρέων ἐταράχθησαν, καὶ ἐσαλεύθησαν, ὅτι ὠργίσθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεός. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 22:8: Καὶ ἐταράχθη καὶ ἐσείσθη ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὰ θεμέλια τοῦ οὐρανοῦ συνεταράχθησαν καὶ ἐσπαράχθησαν, ὃτι ἐθυμώθη Κύριος αὐτοῖς. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA017.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA22.htm.

KJV 2 Samuel 22:8: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:8: [וַתְגָּעַשׁ כ] (וַיִּתְגָּעַ֤שׁ ק) וַתִּרְעַשׁ֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ מֹוסְדֹ֥ות הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַיִּֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ כִּֽי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃. reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The two songs run in step: the earth shook and trembled, the foundations moved, because he was wroth. The word that follows “the foundations” differs. Psalm 18 has הָרִ֣ים (mountains or hills), and 2 Samuel 22 has הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם (the heavens). The Greek agrees with each Hebrew in its own place: τῶν ὀρέων (of the mountains) in Psalm 17:8 and τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (of the heaven) in 2 Samuel 22:8. A reader of the two books is told that what shook was the foundations of the hills in one and of heaven in the other.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The two verses are the same line of the same song, introduced in 2 Samuel 22:1 as the words David spoke on the day the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. In Psalm 18 the things that shake are the foundations of the hills (הָרִים). In 2 Samuel 22 they are the foundations of heaven (הַשָּׁמַיִם). Hills belong to the earth and heaven does not, so the two printings do not name the same foundations.

title: “He did fly upon the wings of the wind” (Psalm 18) — “he was seen upon the wings of the wind” (2 Samuel 22)
summary: After “he rode upon a cherub, and did fly”, Psalm 18:10 says he “did fly” on the wings of the wind. 2 Samuel 22:11 says he “was seen” there.
text: KJV Psalm 18:10: “And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind.” KJV 2 Samuel 22:11: “And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: and he was seen upon the wings of the wind.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:11: וַיִּרְכַּ֣ב עַל־כְּ֭רוּב וַיָּעֹ֑ף וַ֝יֵּ֗דֶא עַל־כַּנְפֵי־רֽוּחַ׃ Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:11: וַיִּרְכַּ֥ב עַל־כְּר֖וּב וַיָּעֹ֑ף וַיֵּרָ֖א עַל־כַּנְפֵי־רֽוּחַ׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 17:11: Καὶ ἐπέβη ἐπὶ χερουβὶμ καὶ ἐπετάσθη, ἐπετάσθη ἐπὶ πτερύγων ἀνέμων. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 22:11: Καὶ ἐπεκάθισεν ἐπὶ τῷ χερουβὶν καὶ ἐπετάσθη, καὶ ὤφθη ἐπὶ πτερύγων ἀνέμου. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA017.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA22.htm.
reasoning: Both verses have the same first half (he rode on a cherub and flew). The last verb differs. In the Hebrew of Psalm 18 it is וַ֝יֵּ֗דֶא, and in 2 Samuel 22 it is וַיֵּרָ֖א; the two words differ in one consonant (ד in the Psalm, ר in Samuel). The KJV renders each as its own verb, “did fly” and “was seen”. The Greek follows suit: ἐπετάσθη (he flew) in Psalm 17:11, where the verb repeats the first half of the verse, and ὤφθη (he was seen) in 2 Samuel 22:11. One text says the Lord flew upon the wind, the other that he was seen upon it.

It does not say which verb is the original, that one copy is a scribal error, or that David wrote both. “Flew” and “was seen” are not claimed to be incompatible acts: a being could fly and be seen. The record states only that the two books give different verbs. No tag applies because the KJV, the Hebrew and the Greek agree with each other in each place. title: At the Lord’s rebuke “the channels of waters were seen” (Psalm 18:15); “the channels of the sea appeared” (2 Samuel 22:16)
summary: In the same line of David’s song, Psalm 18:15 has the channels of waters seen, and 2 Samuel 22:16 has the channels of the sea seen.
text: KJV Psalm 18:15: “Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:16: וַיֵּ֤רָא֨וּ ׀ אֲפִ֥יקֵי מַ֗יִם וַֽיִּגָּלוּ֮ מֹוסְדֹ֪ות תֵּ֫בֵ֥ל מִגַּעֲרָ֣תְךָ֣ יְהוָ֑ה מִ֝נִּשְׁמַ֗ת ר֣וּחַ אַפֶּֽךָ׃. KJV 2 Samuel 22:16: “And the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the Lord, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:16: וַיֵּֽרָאוּ֙ אֲפִ֣קֵי יָ֔ם יִגָּל֖וּ מֹסְדֹ֣ות תֵּבֵ֑ל בְּגַעֲרַ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה מִנִּשְׁמַ֖ת ר֥וּחַ אַפֹּֽו׃. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA018.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/2SA22.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/.
reasoning: The line is the same in both books: the channels are seen and the foundations of the world are laid bare at the Lord’s rebuke. The noun whose channels are seen differs: מַיִם, waters, in Psalm 18 and יָם, sea, in 2 Samuel 22. Waters in general and the sea are not the same thing, and the two printings do not name the same channels.

title: “All nations shall flow unto it” (Isaiah) — “people shall flow unto it” (Micah): the same vision with “nations” and “people” exchanged
summary: Isaiah 2 and Micah 4 give almost the same vision of the mountain of the Lord. In the KJV, Isaiah says all nations flow to the mountain and many people go up, while Micah says people flow to it and many nations come; Isaiah’s Lord rebukes many people, while Micah’s rebukes strong nations afar off. The Hebrew words are not the same in the two books at these points.

KJV Isaiah 2:3: “And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” KJV Micah 4:2: “And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 2:3: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֗ים וְאָמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹרֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיֹּון֙ תֵּצֵ֣א תֹורָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃. Hebrew (WLC) Micah 4:2: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ גֹּויִ֣ם רַבִּ֗ים וְאָֽמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה וְאֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹורֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹֽרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיֹּון֙ תֵּצֵ֣א  תֹורָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃. KJV Isaiah 2:4: “and shall rebuke many people”. KJV Micah 4:3: “and rebuke strong nations afar off”. Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 2:4: וְשָׁפַט֙ בֵּ֣ין הַגֹּויִ֔ם וְהֹוכִ֖יחַ לְעַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבֹותָ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֹֽותֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵרֹ֔ות לֹא־יִשָּׂ֨א גֹ֤וי אֶל־גֹּוי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּ עֹ֖וד מִלְחָמָֽה׃  פ. Hebrew (WLC) Micah 4:3: וְשָׁפַ֗ט בֵּ֚ין עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים וְהֹוכִ֛יחַ לְגֹויִ֥ם עֲצֻמִ֖ים עַד־רָחֹ֑וק וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבֹתֵיהֶ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵרֹ֔ות לֹֽא־יִשְׂא֞וּ גֹּ֤וי אֶל־גֹּוי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּן עֹ֖וד מִלְחָמָֽה׃. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/2/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/33/4/.
reasoning: The two passages run in the same order and share most of their wording, but the nouns for the peoples differ. Isaiah has all the nations (כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם) flowing and many peoples (עַמִּים רַבִּים) saying “Come”; Micah has peoples (עַמִּים) flowing and many nations (גּוֹיִם רַבִּים) saying “Come”. In Isaiah the Lord rebukes many peoples (לְעַמִּים רַבִּים); in Micah he rebukes strong nations afar off (לְגוֹיִם עֲצֻמִּים עַד־רָחוֹק). scope: This is a direct wording contrast between two passages, KJV against KJV, shown with the Hebrew beside it. It is untagged: no translation difference is claimed, because the KJV renders each Hebrew word by its usual English word. The record does not say which book quotes the other, whether both draw on a third source, or that the nations/peoples distinction carries a different doctrine; in Hebrew poetry גּוֹיִם and עַמִּים often stand in parallel and may mean much the same. The record also does not treat Micah’s extra verse 4 as a conflict. The Joel 3:10 record is a separate comparison with the same swords and plowshares wording. title: “For Isaiah had said” and “Hezekiah also had said” — the Hebrew has “And Isaiah said” and “And Hezekiah said”
summary: The KJV of Isaiah 38:21–22 puts the two speeches in the past perfect: “For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs … Hezekiah also had said, What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?” The Hebrew has וַיֹּאמֶר יְשַׁעְיָהוּ and וַיֹּאמֶר חִזְקִיָּהוּ, “And Isaiah said … And Hezekiah said”, with no “for” and no “had”. Brenton’s Greek has Καὶ εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας … Καὶ εἶπεν Ἐζεκίας, the plain past.
text: KJV Isaiah 38:21: “For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover.” KJV Isaiah 38:22: “Hezekiah also had said, What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 38:21: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְשַׁעְיָ֔הוּ יִשְׂא֖וּ דְּבֶ֣לֶת תְּאֵנִ֑ים וְיִמְרְח֥וּ עַֽל־הַשְּׁחִ֖ין וְיֶֽחִי׃ Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 38:22: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ מָ֣ה אֹ֑ות כִּ֥י אֶעֱלֶ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 38:21: Καὶ εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας πρὸς Ἐζεκίαν, λάβε παλάθην ἐκ σύκων, καὶ τρίψον, καὶ κατάπλασαι, καὶ ὑγιὴς ἔσῃ. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 38:22: Καὶ εἶπεν Ἐζεκίας, τοῦτο σημεῖον πρὸς Ἐζεκίαν, ὅτι ἀναβήσομαι εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/38/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA38.htm.
reasoning: In 2 Kings 20:7–8 the same two speeches stand in order: Isaiah calls for the figs and Hezekiah afterwards asks for the sign. In Isaiah 38 they stand last, after the sign (38:7–8) and Hezekiah’s writing. The KJV’s “had said” turns the last two verses into a look back to events already narrated, which removes the difference of order. The Hebrew and the Greek do not carry a look back; the verbs read as the plain past. (Brenton’s English of the Greek also says “had said”, but that is its translator’s English; the Greek is καὶ εἶπεν.)
scope: T applies at 38:21–22 only. The difference found is between the KJV and the Hebrew and Greek. The English past perfect can be a fair way to render a Hebrew narrative tense that follows an earlier event, so the KJV reading is possible; the record says only that the Hebrew and the Greek carry no “had” and no “for”. The record does not say that the order in Isaiah 38 is the order in which the events happened. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and this record compares the wording of the texts and does not show which reading is original.

title: Nathan is told to ask “Shalt thou build me an house?” — Brenton’s Greek prints a flat “thou shalt not build”
summary: KJV 2 Samuel 7:5 puts the Lord’s words as a question. The Hebrew opens with the question particle (הַאַתָּה); Brenton’s Greek prints οὐ σὺ οἰκοδομήσεις, “not you shall build”, a statement.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 7:5: “Go and tell my servant David, Thus saith the Lord, Shalt thou build me an house for me to dwell in?” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 7:5: לֵ֤ךְ וְאָֽמַרְתָּ֙ אֶל־עַבְדִּ֣י אֶל־דָּוִ֔ד כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה הַאַתָּ֛ה תִּבְנֶה־לִּ֥י בַ֖יִת לְשִׁבְתִּֽי׃ [… Thus says the Lord: [is it] you [who] will build me a house for my dwelling?]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 7:5: καὶ εἶπον πρὸς τὸν δοῦλόν μου Δαυὶδ, τάδε λέγει Κύριος, οὐ σὺ οἰκοδομήσεις μοι οἶκον τοῦ κατοικῆσαί με. [… Thus says the Lord: not you shall build me a house for me to dwell in.] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/2SA07.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA07.htm.
reasoning: The KJV and the Hebrew word-for-word carry an interrogative; the Greek page carries a negated statement with no question word. In the Greek the sentence refuses; in the Hebrew and KJV the sentence asks.
scope: T applies at 2 Samuel 7:5 only and compares the sentence form: question in the KJV and Hebrew, statement in the Greek. A rhetorical question can convey a refusal, so the two forms could carry one meaning; this record does not say the Hebrew question is not a refusal, which form is original, or that the KJV mistranslates. title: Fetching the ark: the whole congregation “from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath” — or “the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand”?
summary: In 1 Chronicles 13 David takes counsel with the captains and gathers all Israel from Egypt to Hemath. In 2 Samuel 6:1 he gathers “the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand”.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 13:1: “And David consulted with the captains of thousands and hundreds, and with every leader.” Hebrew (WLC) 13:1: וַיִּוָּעַ֣ץ דָּוִ֗יד עִם־שָׂרֵ֧י הָאֲלָפִ֛ים וְהַמֵּאֹ֖ות לְכָל־נָגִֽיד׃ KJV 1 Chronicles 13:5: “So David gathered all Israel together, from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath, to bring the ark of God from Kirjathjearim.” Hebrew (WLC) 13:5: וַיַּקְהֵ֤ל דָּוִיד֙ אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִן־שִׁיחֹ֥ור מִצְרַ֖יִם וְעַד־לְבֹ֣וא חֲמָ֑ת לְהָבִיא֙ אֶת־אֲרֹ֣ון הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים מִקִּרְיַ֖ת יְעָרִֽים׃ KJV 2 Samuel 6:1: “Again, David gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.” Hebrew (WLC) 6:1: וַיֹּ֨סֶף עֹ֥וד דָּוִ֛ד אֶת־כָּל־בָּח֥וּר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אָֽלֶף׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 6:1: Καὶ συνήγαγεν ἔτι Δαυὶδ πάντα νεανίαν ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, ὡς ἑβδομήκοντα χιλιάδας. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/1CH13.htm, https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/2SA06.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/6/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA06.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/2SA06.htm.
reasoning: Both books tell the first attempt to bring the ark from the house of Abinadab. Chronicles names the gathered body “all Israel”, from the Egyptian border to the entry of Hemath, after a council with the captains of thousands and hundreds; the body is not given a number. Samuel gives it as the chosen men of Israel and a number, thirty thousand, and has no council. The two describe the assembly by different terms.

The two descriptions may be compatible (30,000 chosen men could be the delegation of all Israel), and 1 Chronicles 13:6 and 2 Samuel 6:2 agree that “all Israel” and “all the people” went up. The record states the contrast in wording and the one figure, and does not say the accounts conflict. Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 6:1 has “about seventy thousand” young men (ὡς ἑβδομήκοντα χιλιάδας) where the Hebrew and KJV have thirty thousand; that Greek reading has its own record (`thirty-thousand-chosen-men-or-seventy-thousand-young-men-2-samuel-6-1-greek`). title: “Burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings” — Brenton’s Greek prints “manna”
summary: The KJV of Jeremiah 17:26 lists burnt offerings, sacrifices, meat offerings and incense. The Greek printed lists ὁλοκαυτώματα, θυσίας, θυμιάματα, μάννα and λίβανον, that is, burnt offerings, sacrifices, incense, manna and frankincense.
text: KJV Jeremiah 17:26: “And they shall come from the cities of Judah, and from the places about Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin, and from the plain, and from the mountains, and from the south, bringing burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings, and incense, and bringing sacrifices of praise, unto the house of the Lord.” Hebrew (WLC) 17:26: וּבָ֣אוּ מֵעָרֵֽי־יְ֠הוּדָה וּמִסְּבִיבֹ֨ות יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם וּמֵאֶ֣רֶץ בִּנְיָמִ֗ן וּמִן־הַשְּׁפֵלָ֤ה וּמִן־הָהָר֙ וּמִן־הַנֶּ֔גֶב מְבִאִ֛ים עֹולָ֥ה וְזֶ֖בַח וּמִנְחָ֣ה וּלְבֹונָ֑ה וּמְבִאֵ֥י תֹודָ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה׃ Brenton’s Greek 17:26: Καὶ ἥξουσιν ἐκ τῶν πόλεων Ἰούδα, καὶ κυκλόθεν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ ἐκ γῆς Βενιαμὶν, καὶ ἐκ γῆς πεδινῆς, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ὄρους, καὶ ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Νότον, φέροντες ὁλοκαυτώματα καὶ θυσίας καὶ θυμιάματα καὶ μάννα καὶ λίβανον, φέροντες αἴνεσιν εἰς οἶκον Κυρίου. [bringing whole burnt offerings and sacrifices and incense and manna and frankincense, bringing praise to the house of the Lord] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/24/17/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JER17.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew edition quoted prints עֹלָה וְזֶבַח וּמִנְחָה וּלְבֹונָה, and the KJV renders מִנְחָה “meat offerings”. The Greek printed puts μάννα, the word used for the food in the wilderness, in that position, and has frankincense and incense as separate items. So the KJV and the Greek print different words in the list.
scope: T applies at Jeremiah 17:26 and to the list of what is brought. The record does not say what the Hebrew word means or how the Greek word was chosen. The record is limited to this verse.  This compares the wording of the texts quoted. It does not show which wording is original. The book is prophecy in verse and sermon; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek quoted is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original, and the record does not claim the Greek is a mistranslation of the Hebrew. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
